title: Finding Maximum Streak of Consecutive Login Days
description: For each user, find their **longest streak of consecutive daily logins**. Use the classic technique of subtracting a row number from the login date to group consecutive dates, then finding the max group size per user.
solution_sql: WITH numbered AS (SELECT user_id, login_date, login_date - CAST(ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS INT) AS grp FROM user_logins), streaks AS (SELECT user_id, grp, COUNT(*) AS streak_length FROM numbered GROUP BY user_id, grp) SELECT user_id, MAX(streak_length) AS max_streak FROM streaks GROUP BY user_id ORDER BY max_streak DESC, user_id

test_cases.description: User 2: longest streak=5 (Jan 1-5). User 1: longest streak=3 (Jan 1-3). User 3: longest streak=1 (all isolated days).

hints: Subtract the row number (ordered by date within user) from the login_date — consecutive dates get the same value for this expression, forming a natural group_id.
Count the size of each group (streak) in a second CTE, then take MAX per user to find the longest streak.
explanation: The key insight: if you subtract an ascending row number from a date, consecutive dates produce the same constant value. User 1: Jan 1-rn1=Dec31, Jan 2-rn2=Dec31, Jan 3-rn3=Dec31 (streak of 3, grp=Dec31). Jan 5-rn4=Jan1 (gap broke it), Jan 7-rn5=Jan2, Jan 8-rn6=Jan2 (streak of 2). Max=3. User 2: Jan 1-5 all get grp=Dec31 (streak=5). User 3: all non-consecutive → all different grp values, max streak=1.
